summary: The active pricing-engine config change cfg-3120 — ramping flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5% to 100% at 12:04:00Z — is the identified root cause of the order-service quote timeouts, at medium confidence (0.60). The chain is temporally tight and mechanism-specific: pricing-engine CPU stepped from ~40% to ~99-100% and p99 from ~60ms to ~2.5-2.8s only in the minute bucket following the ramp, with GreeksV2-named WARN/ERROR logs; order-service, the synchronous caller, shows a propagated 2500ms client-side timeout with flat local CPU. The competing hypotheses are contradicted by evidence: the market-data-service protobuf deploy (dep-6111, 11:56Z) produced no latency step anywhere including in market-data-service itself, redis-cache is healthy on every exposed metric, and neither pricing-engine nor order-service request_rate shows any traffic surge. The load-bearing unmeasured hop remains that GreeksV2's Monte-Carlo calculator is materially more expensive per quote than v1; that assumption plus unresolved change-management/log telemetry keeps confidence at medium rather than high.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Greeks v2 feature-flag ramp to 100% makes every quote run the expensive Monte-Carlo path, saturating pricing-engine CPU and timing out the quote path
ranked_hypotheses.statement: cfg-3120 ramped pricing-engine flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct from 5% to 100% at 12:04:00Z. The GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo calculator (20000 paths) is far more expensive per quote than the v1 path; once it applies to all quote traffic, pricing-engine CPU saturates at ~99-100%, per-request compute exceeds the internal 2000ms deadline and the caller's 2500ms budget, so pricing-engine quote calls time out. order-service, which calls pricing-engine synchronously at its quote step, surfaces those as client-side 'timed out after 2500ms' errors and ~8% error_rate with flat local CPU. The fault originates in the pricing-engine config change, not in any code release.

causal_chain.claim: cfg-3120 ramps flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5 -> 100 on pricing-engine at 12:04:00Z

The ramp step is the only change aligned to the onset: pricing-engine CPU/latency sit at their exact 38-42% / 57-63ms baselines for the whole 11:50-12:04Z interval (including the 11:56Z deploy minute) and step only in the 12:05Z bucket (CPU ->98.65 avg, p99 ->2534.9), with request_rate flat throughout so no traffic change accompanies the step

pricing-engine begins evaluating the expensive GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path (paths=20000) for essentially all quote requests instead of ~5%, producing the explicit 'took 6465ms' WARN from 12:05:21Z and 56 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' ERRORs
CPU saturation at 99-100% is concomitant with the latency jump (~40x p99 to ~2.6s) and pricing-engine error_rate confirms the same boundary (clean 0.13-0.32% through 12:05Z, then ~13% from 12:06Z)

order-service, calling pricing-engine over http at the quote step, records client-side 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' (67 from 12:06:10Z), p99 ~2306ms and ~8% error_rate, while order-service's own CPU stays flat ~39-41%

Blast radius is confined to the pricing-engine -> order-service path: market-data-service p99 flat ~39ms, api-gateway flat ~205-220ms, redis-cache healthy on all exposed metrics (hit_ratio, evictions, clients, cpu) — consistent with a pricing-engine-local fault
No recovery occurs: pricing-engine CPU still 98.65-100%, p99 ~2542-2618ms and order-service error_rate ~8% at the end of data (13:57Z), and no rollback is evidenced

assumptions: GreeksV2's Monte-Carlo calculator is materially more expensive per quote than the v1 path. This is the single load-bearing hop and is NOT directly measured: the explicit 'Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms' WARN and the 2000ms budget-exceeded ERRORs name GreeksV2, and pre-ramp CPU/latency are flat, but no per-path cost measurement exists.
The flag is traffic-weighted and global at 100% (no per-symbol gating that could produce a slow ramp).

The 60s CPU/latency series (F30/F31/F32) is the discriminator the critic asked for: it shows no step at 11:56Z and a step only in the 12:05Z bucket, so a pre-ramp baseline for the 11:56-12:04Z interval effectively exists even though the earlier baseline (F10) straddled the deploy.

ranked_hypotheses.title: market-data-service protobuf serialization change (dep-6111) degrades the pricing-engine call path with a lagged effect
ranked_hypotheses.statement: dep-6111 at 11:56:00Z switched market-data-service quote serialization to protobuf. If the new serialization produces larger payloads, incompatible framing, or extra deserialization cost on the consumer, pricing-engine's market-data-service calls would slow (or back-pressure would build), driving pricing-engine CPU/latency up and propagating to order-service quote timeouts. This is the reporter's suspicion. Its residual plausibility rests on a ~9-minute lag between the deploy and onset.

causal_chain.claim: dep-6111 switches market-data-service quote serialization to protobuf at 11:56:00Z, remaining live with rolled_back_at null
The new serialization degrades the pricing-engine -> market-data-service call (payload size/framing/deserialization cost), but only manifests after a warm-up/accumulation lag of ~9 minutes
pricing-engine latency and CPU rise as a consequence of slower upstream calls rather than local compute
order-service quote-step timeouts follow from pricing-engine slowness

assumptions: The protobuf change degrades rather than improves the market-data-service response path — no evidence of any such degradation exists; market-data-service's own p99 is flat at ~39ms across the deploy boundary.
The change has a ~9-minute delayed effect. This is asserted only to preserve the hypothesis, not evidenced.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: Direct evidence contradicts it: pricing-engine CPU and latency are flat at baseline (38-42% / 57-63ms) for the entire 11:50-12:04Z interval INCLUDING the 11:56Z deploy minute, and the step occurs only in the 12:05Z bucket (F30/F31/F32). market-data-service's own p99 is flat at ~39ms across the deploy (F25/F28), so the change produced no latency effect anywhere it would have shown one. The mechanism the failure reports names GreeksV2 (calculator=GreeksV2), not serialization (F10). The 9-minute quiet gap after dep-6111 with zero downstream effect anywhere in the stack is decisive against it. (Note: the critic's point that market-data-service metrics were incompletely queried is now partly answered — its p99 was obtained and is flat.)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared redis-cache degradation on the pricing/quote path drives latency and retry CPU
ranked_hypotheses.statement: redis-cache is shared:true and reachable from both pricing-engine and market-data-service, so it sits on the common quote path. A redis-cache degradation (failover/miss storm/hot key, as in HIST-107) could inflate pricing-engine latency and CPU via cache-miss amplification and retries, and propagate to order-service quote timeouts without any direct fault in order-service or market-data-service.

causal_chain.claim: redis-cache is a shared datastore reached by both pricing-engine and market-data-service, giving it reach into the quote path
redis-cache degrades (failover/miss storm/hot key) in the 12:05Z window
pricing-engine suffers cache-miss amplification and retry CPU cost, saturating CPU and raising p99
order-service quote-step timeouts follow from pricing-engine slowness

assumptions: No change touched redis-cache, so this requires spontaneous infra degradation.

A shared-store event could produce exactly the GreeksV2-specific WARN/ERROR signature (calculator=GreeksV2, 2000ms budget) — it could not explain why the failure text names a calculator introduced by a config change.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: The critic asked for the redis-cache telemetry; it now exists and contradicts the hypothesis. Across 11:30-13:00Z redis-cache is healthy on every exposed metric: hit_ratio 95.45-96.73%, evictions ~2.3-3.6/min, connected_clients ~296-320, cpu ~21-23% — no failover, miss storm or eviction spike at 11:56Z or 12:04-12:05Z (F26). The pricing-engine failure text is calculator=GreeksV2 with a 2000ms compute budget exceeded (F10), a CPU-bound compute signature, not cache-miss amplification. A spontaneous store degradation coinciding with the 12:04Z flag ramp is also unsupported by any change record (F13). (Residual caveat: redis-cache exposes no latency series, so a purely server-side latency event cannot be 100% excluded — this keeps a floor under the confidence rather than zero.)

ranked_hypotheses.title: Capacity saturation: market-open-style quote volume outgrew pricing-engine provisioning (HIST-113 analogue)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: pricing-engine's CPU saturating to 99-100% with quote timeouts mirrors HIST-113 ('pricing-engine CPU saturation at market open', capacity_saturation). Under this hypothesis a genuine traffic surge exceeded provisioned pricing-engine capacity independent of any specific change; the coincident cfg-3120 and dep-6111 are incidental.

causal_chain.claim: pricing-engine CPU saturates to ~99-100% with quote timeouts (same service+ symptom as HIST-113)
A market-open-style traffic surge exceeds provisioned pricing-engine capacity
order-service quote-step timeouts follow from pricing-engine saturation

assumptions: Traffic volume rose materially at 12:04-12:05Z. This is now directly refuted, not merely absent.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: The critic's requested traffic series now exists and refutes the surge premise. pricing-engine request_rate is flat ~590-687 req/s across 11:50-12:20Z with no step at 12:04-12:05Z (12:02Z 667 / 12:04Z 625 / 12:06Z 667) (F34), and order-service request_rate is likewise flat ~212-256 req/s with no surge at the ramp (F35). A capacity cause requires a volume step that did not occur; CPU saturation arrived with traffic unchanged, which is only explicable by a change in per-request cost (the flag ramp). HIST-113 remains an analogy, but the mechanism it requires is absent here.

facts.statement: Exactly one deployment and one config change occurred in the incident window: dep-6111 market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' at 11:56:00Z (author v.rao, live, not rolled back) and cfg-3120 pricing-engine flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5 -> 100 at 12:04:00Z (author pm-experiments).

Dependency direction is order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service (http); order-service has no direct edge to market-data-service or redis-cache, making pricing-engine the only shared component on the quote path and redis-cache the only shared datastore reachable from it.

pricing-engine CPU and latency were flat at baseline for the entire 11:50-12:04Z interval at 60s resolution, INCLUDING the 11:56Z deploy minute (CPU ~38-42%, p99 ~57-63ms); the step occurs only in the 12:05Z bucket, jumping to ~98.65% avg CPU and ~2535-2849ms p99.

pricing-engine emits WARN 'GreeksV2Calculator: Monte-Carlo paths=20000 took 6465ms for symbol opt-41547' from 12:05:21Z and ERROR 'request deadline exceeded computing quote (2000ms budget) calculator=GreeksV2' (56 occurrences) from 12:06:41Z, coincident with CPU going 40% -> ~99-100% and p99 ~2.6s.

order-service shows a propagated failure, not a local resource problem: p99 breaks out of its ~148-154ms baseline to 2306ms avg / 3011ms max in the 12:05Z bucket and stays ~2800-3000ms; error_rate rises from ~0.2% to 6.53% (max 8.37%) and plateaus ~8%; the signature is a client-side 'pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms' (67 occurrences from 12:06:10Z), with order-service CPU flat at ~39-41% throughout.
market-data-service p99 is flat at ~39-40ms across the entire 11:30-13:00Z window, with no deviation at the 11:56Z protobuf deploy or the 12:04-12:05Z window (max never exceeds 43.28ms).

redis-cache is healthy on every exposed metric across 11:30-13:00Z: hit_ratio 95.45-96.73%, evictions ~2.3-3.6/min, connected_clients ~296-320, cpu ~21-23%, with no failover, miss-storm or eviction spike at 11:56Z or 12:04-12:05Z.

No traffic surge occurred: pricing-engine request_rate is flat ~590-687 req/s across 11:50-12:20Z including across the 12:04Z ramp (12:02Z 667 / 12:04Z 625 / 12:06Z 667), and order-service request_rate is flat ~212-256 req/s with no step at the ramp.

Blast radius is confined to the pricing-engine -> order-service path: api-gateway p99 is flat ~205-220ms and market-data-service flat ~39ms through the 12:05Z bucket; only order-service and pricing-engine show the step.

No recovery occurred through the end of data: at 13:54-13:57Z pricing-engine CPU is still 98.65-100%, p99 2542-2618ms (~43x the 59ms baseline), and order-service error_rate still ~8%; no rollback text appears in readable pricing-engine or order-service logs.

Historical context: HIST-113 shares the pricing-engine + 'quote timeouts'/'cpu 99%' symptom but had a capacity root cause; HIST-116 is the only protocol/serialization-change root cause in the result set; HIST-107 was a redis failover cache-miss storm. None matches the present mechanism.

assumptions: ASSUMPTION: GreeksV2's Monte-Carlo calculator (paths=20000) is materially more expensive per quote than the v1 path, so applying it to 100% of quote traffic raises per-request cost enough to blow the 2000ms internal deadline and the caller's 2500ms budget. This is the single load-bearing hop and is NOT directly measured — no per-path cost measurement exists; it rests on the GreeksV2-named WARN/ERROR text plus flat pre-ramp CPU/latency.

ASSUMPTION: cfg-3120 is traffic-weighted and global at 100%, with no per-symbol gating that could produce a slow ramp; the step-shaped onset in the 12:03-12:05Z buckets is consistent with immediate 100% application.

ASSUMPTION: The flat pricing-engine CPU/latency series from 11:50Z through the 12:04Z minute constitutes a valid pre-ramp baseline, so the one-minute separation between the 12:04:00Z config change and the first anomaly is meaningful rather than coincidental (the metric buckets are 300s wide, so the exact sub-minute ordering of cfg-3120 vs first deviation is not resolvable).

ASSUMPTION: The blast-radius negative results (market-data-service, redis-cache, api-gateway flat) plus the absence of any other change in the window are sufficient to exclude the competing hypotheses, notwithstanding that portfolio-service, exchange-gateway, kafka and ledger-db were never tested.

ASSUMPTION: No further deployment or config change affecting the quote path occurred in the window; this relies on the config-audit shard 2/3 gap (tc-002 partial) having been cured by the retry (tc-009), which is not proven for the full 11:00-12:16Z window across all services.

timeline.event: dep-6111 deployed: market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf' (author v.rao). No subsequent latency effect anywhere in the stack.
pricing-engine CPU (~38-42%) and p99 (~57-63ms) remain flat at baseline at 60s resolution, including the deploy minute; market-data-service p99 flat ~39ms; redis-cache healthy.

recommended_actions.action: Immediately revert cfg-3120 on pricing-engine: set flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct back from 100 to 5 (its pre-incident value). Do not roll back dep-6111 (market-data-service protobuf), which evidence clears.
recommended_actions.rationale: cfg-3120 is the only change temporally aligned with onset (12:04:00Z vs first anomaly in the 12:05Z bucket, first GreeksV2 WARN 12:05:21Z); reverting restores the cheap v1 quote path that held ~40% CPU / ~60ms p99. Both H1's flag-ramp mechanism and the clearing of H2 require this test.

recommended_actions.action: After the flag revert, verify recovery on the discriminating series at 60s resolution: pricing-engine cpu_pct should fall back to ~38-42% and latency_p99_ms to ~57-63ms, order-service error_rate to ~0.2% and p99 to ~148-154ms — no later than the minute bucket following the revert. This doubles as the final confirmation of the root cause and as the inverse of the observed step.
recommended_actions.rationale: Latency and CPU are still fully saturated at 13:54-13:57Z with no step-down, so the mitigation must be measured against the exact baselines observed pre-ramp; a step-down confirms H1, a failure to step down falsifies it.

recommended_actions.action: Preserve evidence and open a config-change record for cfg-3120 documenting the revert time, old/new value and the observed metric response; capture the effective flag value directly from pricing-engine runtime state (e.g. its flags endpoint) since config-change logs are not readable.
recommended_actions.rationale: config-service and deployment-service log namespaces do not exist and no rollback text appears in readable logs, so the change-management trail must be reconstructed from the flag system itself to close the change-control loop.

recommended_actions.action: Instrument and measure per-path quote cost before re-ramping Greeks v2: add timing/cost histograms split by calculator (GreeksV2 vs v1) and by symbols configured for v2, and run a canary to build a cost-delta curve versus rollout_pct (e.g. 5/25/50/100).
recommended_actions.rationale: The load-bearing unverified hop is that GreeksV2 (Monte-Carlo paths=20000) is materially more expensive per quote than v1; the WARN shows a 6465ms Monte-Carlo call but no controlled per-path cost measurement exists, so the ramp must be gated on measured cost.

recommended_actions.action: Re-run the exhausted discriminating queries so remaining hypotheses can be fully closed: pricing-engine request_rate at 60s resolution over 11:30-13:00Z (to exclude a sub-120s traffic burst), market-data-service cpu_pct and request_rate, portfolio-service latency_p99_ms, exchange-gateway metrics, order-service db_pool_in_use, and the config-audit shard 2/3 coverage for the full 11:00-12:16Z window.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2/H3/H4 are refuted by available evidence but a residual floor remains because market-data-service resource metrics, portfolio-service/exchange-gateway, the MySQL-pool check and part of the audit shard coverage were never obtained.

recommended_actions.action: Widen metric retention/resolution around config and deploy events to sub-minute (currently 300s buckets) and add a native redis-cache latency series (currently only connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct).
recommended_actions.rationale: 300s buckets left the exact onset instant and the cfg-3120-vs-first-deviation ordering unresolved, and the absence of a redis latency series prevented fully excluding H3 (which kept a confidence floor under it).

recommended_actions.action: Gate expensive flag rollouts on pricing-engine CPU/latency headroom: require a staged ramp with automatic rollback when cpu_pct crosses a saturation threshold or p99 exceeds an SLO budget during the ramp window.
recommended_actions.rationale: A 5%->100% single-step ramp took pricing-engine from 40% to 99-100% CPU in one minute and propagated to ~8% order-service error rate for hours with no automatic remediation, since no rollback appears in any readable signal.

data_gaps: Change-coverage gap: the first get_config_changes call (tc-002) returned partial:true ('config-audit shard 2/3 did not respond') and the retry returned a single change with partial:false, but shard coverage for all services across 11:00-12:16Z is not proven — additional config/flag changes on order-service, exchange-gateway, api-gateway or shared components cannot be fully ruled out.

No log namespace exposes config-service or deployment-service (both returned unknown service), so cfg-3120's effective value and any rollback of cfg-3120 or dep-6111 cannot be read from log telemetry.

Tool budget was exhausted before several discriminators could be collected: pricing-engine request_rate at 60s resolution (only a 120s series was obtained, which could smear a sub-2-minute spike at 12:04-12:05Z), order-service db_pool_in_use, market-data-service cpu_pct/request_rate, portfolio-service p99 (backend 503), exchange-gateway metrics, and redis-cache/kafka/ledger-db telemetry.
redis-cache exposes no latency or failover/reconnect series, so a purely server-side latency event cannot be fully excluded — only inferred absent from flat hit_ratio, evictions, connections and CPU.

Metric buckets are 300s with no sub-minute points, so the exact onset instant within 12:05:00-12:10:00Z is unresolved and the strict ordering of cfg-3120 (12:04:00Z) versus the first deviation is not provable at 1-second precision.

No per-endpoint or per-call breakdown of pricing-engine traffic exists, so it cannot be directly shown that the flag ramp (rather than a change in call mix) raised per-request cost; request_rate is aggregate only.
No historical incident in the result set has a serialization/payload-change root cause on market-data-service, so precedent analysis is limited to analogies.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Reverting/gating cfg-3120 (greeks_v2 back to 5%) does NOT bring pricing-engine CPU back to ~40% and p99 back to ~60ms — i.e. the fault persists after the flag is restored, in which case the config change is not causal.

A measured per-path cost comparison shows the GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo path is NOT materially more expensive than v1 (e.g. comparable ms/quote at equal concurrency), which would break the single load-bearing hop and require re-attributing the CPU saturation.

A pricing-engine request_rate or per-endpoint series at sub-120s resolution reveals a genuine quote-traffic or per-endpoint-mix surge at 12:04-12:05Z, reviving H4 (capacity saturation) despite the flat aggregate series.

Telemetry from the untested components (market-data-service cpu_pct, portfolio-service, exchange-gateway, kafka, ledger-db) shows a coincident deviation at 12:04-12:05Z, which would widen the blast radius and re-open H2/H3.
Config-audit shard 2/3 coverage reveals an additional change on pricing-engine, order-service or a shared component near onset that also plausibly explains the CPU/latency step.

Evidence emerges that cfg-3120 had already been effectively applied to most quote traffic before 12:04:00Z (e.g. a prior partial ramp), which would remove the temporal alignment between the change and the onset.

findings.statement: Exactly one deployment occurred in 11:00Z-13:59Z across all services: dep-6111, market-data-service v5.2.0 'Switch quote serialization to protobuf', deployed_at 2026-05-20T11:56:00Z, author v.rao, status live and rolled_back_at null.

One config change in the window: cfg-3120 on pricing-engine, key flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct, old_value 5 -> new_value 100, changed_at 2026-05-20T12:04:00Z, author pm-experiments ('Ramp Greeks v2 experiment to all traffic') — 8 minutes AFTER the market-data-service deploy and 12 minutes before the 12:16Z report.

Dependency edges are caller -> callee: order-service -> pricing-engine (http), and pricing-engine -> market-data-service (http), so market-data-service is UPSTREAM of pricing-engine which is directly upstream of order-service; order-service has no direct edge to market-data-service.

market-data-service is not a leaf: it also serves api-gateway and portfolio-service (http) and depends on shared redis-cache (cache) and exchange-gateway (http); shared datastores used by multiple services are redis-cache, ledger-db and kafka (marked shared:true).

dep-6111 (market-data-service protobuf serialization) is timestamped 11:56:00Z, which PRECEDES the onset of the first anomalies in the 12:05Z bucket by roughly 9-10 minutes; it remained live with rolled_back_at null.

cfg-3120 (pricing-engine greeks_v2 rollout ramped 5->100) is timestamped 12:04:00Z, which is the change aligning closest to the 12:05Z onset bucket — ~1 minute before pricing-engine's first WARN at 12:05:21Z. It is 8 minutes AFTER the market-data-service deploy.

The dependency path common to both order-service and pricing-engine: order-service calls pricing-engine (http); pricing-engine calls redis-cache (cache) and market-data-service (http); order-service's own downstream edges are ledger-db, pricing-engine, exchange-gateway and kafka. So order-service has no direct edge to market-data-service or redis-cache — pricing-engine is the only shared component sitting on both quotepaths, and redis-cache is the only shared datastore reachable from the pricing path.

Historical leads: HIST-113 (2026-01-28) shares pricing-engine + 'quote timeouts'/'cpu 99%' symptoms but its root cause was capacity saturation; HIST-107 (2025-12-09) involved redis-cache + market-data-service with 'cache miss storm'/'quote latency' from a Redis failover. These are leads only, not evidence about the current cause.

findings.statement: No rollback text appears in pricing-engine WARN+ logs or order-service WARN+ logs for 12:04-13:59Z (both queries returned total_matched 0, truncated false). The config-service and deployment-service log namespaces do not exist (unknown service), so config/deploy rollback events cannot be read from log telemetry.

pricing-engine cpu_pct is still fully saturated through the end of data: 3-minute buckets show avg 98.65/max 99.24 at 13:54Z and avg 99.33/max 100.0 at 13:57Z — no recovery, no step-down that would indicate a config/rollback taking effect.

pricing-engine latency_p99_ms remains elevated at the end of the window: 2542.5ms (avg) at 13:54Z and 2618.05ms at 13:57Z, versus a 12:00Z baseline of 59.07ms — roughly 43x baseline, unchanged in character since onset.
order-service error_rate stays plateaued at ~8% through 13:57Z (13:54Z avg 8.18/max 8.87; 13:57Z avg 8.29/max 8.6) against a 12:00Z baseline of 0.25% — the failure is not clearing.

The step into saturation occurred in the 12:03Z bucket, not 12:05Z at this granularity: pricing-engine cpu_pct 12:03Z avg 59.02/max 98.65 and latency_p99_ms 12:03Z avg 884.08/max 2534.9, i.e. the first bucket with a max already at saturation — consistent with the 12:04:00Z cfg-3120 change falling inside/at the edge of the 12:03Z-12:06Z bucket.

No post-12:04Z rollback (of dep-6111 or cfg-3120) is evidenced by any signal I could read: metrics never step back down, and no rollback-tagged log exists in the readable service namespaces. Whether the change-management system recorded a rollback or a new cfg-3120 value cannot be verified from log telemetry.

market-data-service latency_p99_ms does NOT deviate at 11:56Z (the protobuf deploy) or in the 12:04-12:05Z window: it holds a flat 39-40ms across the entire 11:30-13:00Z window (e.g. 39.06ms avg at 11:58Z, 39.43ms at 12:06Z, max never exceeds 43.28ms). The dep-6111 protobuf serialization change produced no latency step in market-data-service itself.

redis-cache is healthy on every metric available across 11:30-13:00Z: hit_ratio_pct stays 95.45-96.73% (96.73% at 12:06Z), evictions_per_min stays ~2.3-3.6 (3.27 at 12:06Z), connected_clients stays ~296-320 (309.61 at 12:06Z), cpu_pct stays ~21-23% (22.41 at 12:06Z). No failover/reconnect, miss-storm or eviction spike at 11:56Z or 12:04-12:05Z. redis-cache exposes only connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct — there is no latency metric.

api-gateway latency_p99_ms shows no independent step in the 12:05Z bucket: it is flat ~205-220ms across 11:30-13:00Z (12:02Z avg 204.48 -> 12:06Z avg 216.47, within normal spread; window max 233.77ms). It does not share the order-service/pricing-engine failure signature.

market-data-service is not resource-constrained and shows no deviation in the 12:04-12:05Z window on the metric it does expose: its p99, and cpu/request_rate are the only series available (cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts). The flat p99 across the deploy boundary means the protobuf change did not inflate market-data-service's own serving latency in this window.

The blast-radius claim is NOT supported by the two shared components reachable from the other services: market-data-service (shared upstream of pricing-engine, api-gateway, portfolio-service) is flat at ~39ms and api-gateway is flat at ~210ms through the 12:05Z bucket, so only the pricing-engine->order-service path shows the step. Neither market-data-service nor redis-cache shows any deviation at the two candidate change times (11:56Z deploy, 12:04-12:05Z ramp).

pricing-engine cpu_pct was FLAT at its ~38-42% baseline for the entire 11:50:00-12:04:00Z interval at 60s resolution: 11:56Z avg 40.22 (dep-6111 deploy minute), 11:57 40.35, 11:58 41.86, 11:59 38.03, 12:00 41.45, 12:01 39.39, 12:02 40.08, 12:03 40.18, 12:04 38.22. There is NO step at 11:56Z. The step occurs only in the 12:05Z bucket, jumping to avg 98.65 and staying 98-100% through 12:10Z (12:08 and 12:10 = 100.0).

pricing-engine latency_p99_ms was FLAT at its ~57-63ms baseline across the same interval: 11:56Z 56.86, 11:57 60.52, 11:58 60.41, 11:59 57.86, 12:00 60.06, 12:01 58.97, 12:02 58.17, 12:03 56.82, 12:04 60.53. No step at 11:56Z; the jump is in the 12:05Z bucket (avg 2534.9, max 2534.9), continuing 2521.4 (12:06), 2410.97 (12:07) and peaking 2849.25 at 12:08Z.

Answer to the task question: NO — pricing-engine CPU and latency were at baseline for the full 8 minutes between the market-data-service deploy (11:56Z) and the cfg-3120 ramp (12:04Z). Both metrics held ~38-42% CPU and ~57-63ms p99 from 11:50Z through the 12:04Z minute; the step to ~99% CPU / ~2535-2849ms p99 happens in the 12:05Z minute bucket, i.e. the minute immediately AFTER the 12:04Z cfg-3120 ramp, not at 11:56Z.

pricing-engine error_rate confirms the same onset boundary: flat ~0.13-0.32% through 12:05Z (12:04Z 0.29, 12:05Z 0.15), then jumps to 12.98% at 12:06Z and holds 12.43-13.61% through 12:10Z. The 12:05Z bucket itself is still clean, so errors lag the CPU/latency step by one minute.

pricing-engine request_rate shows NO traffic surge — it is flat ~590-687 req/s across 11:50-12:20Z at 120s resolution, including across the 12:04Z ramp: 12:02Z 667.24, 12:04Z 625.14, 12:06Z 666.82, 12:08Z 646.04, 12:10Z 616.42. There is no step-up at 12:04-12:05Z; the highest point (687.48) is at 12:06Z, well within the pre-incident range (11:52Z max 674.47, 12:00Z max 674.54).

order-service request_rate likewise shows NO surge at 12:04-12:05Z: it is flat ~212-256 req/s across 11:30-13:00Z at 120s resolution. Values around the ramp: 12:02Z 242.27, 12:04Z 230.26, 12:06Z 234.78, 12:08Z 231.44, 12:10Z 227.07. The only mild uplifts (253.88 at 12:42Z, 243.09 at 12:40Z, 240.16 at 12:36Z) occur long after onset and are within the overall min 212.2 / max 256.97 range. No quote-traffic surge coincides with 12:04-12:05Z.
